title: Why Did Cao Cao Say He Burned His Own Ships at Red Cliffs?
description:
Winter, 208 AD, on the Yangtze: Cao Cao's warships sat one after another, bow to stern. A few days later they were ash. Afterwards he wrote to Sun Quan and said he had set that fire himself.

This episode starts with the letter Cao Cao sent before the battle, the one about "800,000 marines" coming to "hunt together in Wu": the numbers Zhou Yu ran for Sun Quan, the sickness already spreading through Cao's camp before the fighting began, Huang Gai's fake surrender letter and that day's southeast wind, the one line each of the three histories of Wei, Shu and Wu wrote down, and the muddy road at Huarong, ending with how Cao Cao actually worded his letter after the battle. The parts we know best, the chained ships, the self-inflicted beating, the borrowed east wind and Guan Yu letting Cao Cao go at Huarong, are all plot from the novel Romance of the Three Kingdoms; this episode sets them side by side with what the histories say.

Quotations follow the Wenyuange Siku Quanshu edition of the Records of the Three Kingdoms (with Pei Songzhi's annotations). The source of every quotation, year and number is listed in the references below; sentences that begin "we think" are the channel's view.

The illustrations in this episode are AI-generated. Historical figures are drawn as cartoon characters, unnamed and not meant to resemble anyone.

Information as of 2026-10-19

cb101.text: Winter, 208 AD, on the banks of the Yangtze.

cb102.text: A man past fifty stands on deck, eyeing the far bank.

cb103.text: His warships sit one after another, bow to stern.

cb104.text: A few days later, those ships were nothing but ash.

cb105.text: Oddly, he later wrote his rival,

cb106.text: saying he had set that fire himself.

cb108.text: That winter, in the northern camps, men fell sick one by one.

cb109.text: An old Wu general wrote a surrender letter and sent it to him.

cb111.text: in the records, what was Zhuge Liang up to then?

cb112.text: Who really set the Red Cliffs fire?

cb201.text: Many first think of the novel Romance of the Three Kingdoms.

cb202.text: But it was written over a thousand years after Red Cliffs.

cb301.text: Much closer: the Records of the Three Kingdoms, from decades later.

cb302.text: Its later annotator added records from several old books.

cb304.text: That year, they say, Cao Cao had just taken Jingzhou; Liu Biao's son yielded without a fight.

cb326.text: Overtaken by Cao Cao's cavalry, Liu Bei fled to Xiakou.

cb309.text: He sent a young man to Wu to ask for help.

cb310.text: Zhuge Liang urged Sun Quan to ally with Liu Bei.

cb303.text: Meanwhile, Cao Cao also wrote to Sun Quan.

cb305.text: It said he was coming with 800,000 marines to 'hunt with the General in Wu.'

cb307.text: No need to say who the prey was.

cb308.text: In Wu's court, many urged Sun Quan to surrender.

cb323.text: Lu Su told Sun Quan privately: all of us can surrender; you alone cannot.

cb324.text: We'd keep our posts. Surrender, and where would you go?

cb311.text: A Wu general in his early thirties opposed it too.

cb325.text: Sun Quan's blade lopped off a desk corner: 'Say surrender again and you're next.'

cb313.text: That night Zhou Yu saw Sun Quan alone and ran the numbers.

cb314.text: Northern troops: only 150-160,000, worn out by a long march.

cb315.text: Liu Biao's newly absorbed men: 70-80,000 at most, still wavering.

cb317.text: Zhou Yu said 50,000 crack troops could stop them.

cb318.text: Sun Quan gave 30,000; they set off with Liu Bei's men.

cb320.text: The records say Cao's men were sick before the first clash.

cb321.text: After the first clash, Cao pulled his ships back to the north bank.

cb322.text: Across the river, one glance sparked an idea.

cb401.text: The one who saw it was Huang Gai, a veteran under Zhou Yu.

cb402.text: He said: they're many, we're few; a long war hurts us.

cb403.text: Remember those ships moored bow to stern? Huang Gai said: they'll burn.

cb203.text: In the novel, a strategist tells Cao Cao to chain his ships together.

cb404.text: The records have no such strategist, and no chains.

cb405.text: Huang Gai stuffed dozens of warships with dry straw and wood.

cb407.text: Flags up, from afar they looked like any warship.

cb434.text: Each big ship towed a small fast boat for the escape after the fire.

cb408.text: But first, he wrote to Cao Cao.

cb410.text: It said Wu had shown him great kindness.

cb411.text: Yet anyone could see Jiangdong can't stop the north.

cb412.text: So he'd bring his ships and surrender.

cb437.text: What did Cao Cao make of it?

cb413.text: Cao Cao questioned the messenger in private.

cb414.text: He said: I fear you're tricking me.

cb415.text: If it's true, Huang Gai's reward will top everyone's.

cb207.text: The novel has Huang Gai flogged to fool Cao Cao: the 'bitter flesh ruse.'

cb417.text: The records never mention a flogging.

cb418.text: On the day of battle, a southeast wind blew, and it blew hard.

cb420.text: The novel says Zhuge Liang borrowed this wind at the Seven Stars Altar.

cb435.text: In the records, nobody borrows it.

cb438.text: With wind and ships ready, how to get close to Cao's camp without being seen through?

cb421.text: Ten ships led the way; in midstream, they raised their sails.

cb422.text: Cao's men leaned out, pointing: 'Huang Gai's surrendering!'

cb423.text: Still some way off, the crews lit the fires all at once.

cb424.text: Wind behind them, the ships flew like arrows.

cb425.text: North-bank ships burned; fire hit the camps.

cb426.text: Soon, smoke and flame covered half the sky.

cb436.text: Zhou Yu's elite followed, drums thundering; the north broke.

cb428.text: So what was Zhuge Liang doing? Remember that question?

cb429.text: His biography covers Red Cliffs in just one line.

cb430.text: 'Cao lost at Red Cliffs, led his army to Ye.'

cb431.text: They say only that Zhou Yu's fleet came with him to Liu Bei, not what he did that day.

cb432.text: But on how Cao Cao retreated, the records hide a line few people notice.

cb510.text: It's in the Records' section on Wu: just seven characters.

cb512.text: Cao Cao burned his remaining ships, then left. Remember: he said he set the fire himself?

cb513.text: Eight more characters follow: his men, starving and sick, more than half dead.

cb514.text: We think he likely couldn't take them or leave them to the foe.

cb520.text: Then comes Huarong Road. In the novel, Guan Yu waits there and lets him go.

cb521.text: In the records, just a muddy road horses couldn't cross, in a strong wind.

cb522.text: He had the weak soldiers lay straw so the cavalry could pass.

cb523.text: Past the mud, Cao Cao laughed aloud. His generals asked why.

cb524.text: He said: Liu Bei is my kind of man, just a bit slow with his schemes.

cb530.text: Soon Liu Bei did set fires behind him, but Cao Cao was already past.

cb526.text: He left Cao Ren to hold Jiangling.

cb516.text: At a place called Baqiu, plague struck again; again he burned ships.

cb518.text: Were Guo Jia alive, I'd never have come to this.

cb519.text: Guo Jia, his top adviser, died of illness the year before.

cb527.text: How exactly did he word that letter claiming the fire?

cb601.text: It survives in an old book quoted in the annotations to the Records.

cb602.text: He wrote: at Red Cliffs we met sickness; I burned my own ships and left.

cb603.text: Zhou Yu won that fame for nothing.

cb612.text: The book that records it adds: Zhou Yu was so famous that Cao Cao and Liu Bei both wanted to smear him.

cb604.text: The ten fire ships into Cao's camp? The letter says not a word.

cb501.text: Remember the illness? Cao Cao's annals in the Records give Red Cliffs only 'a setback' and 'a great plague.'

cb613.text: Another old book flatly says Cao's ships were burned by Liu Bei.

cb606.text: We think the two letters work the same way.

cb607.text: The first one, before the battle, inflated his army; this one, after it, shrank his defeat.

cb608.text: So the Red Cliffs fire was set by two men: one to win, one to get away.

cb610.text: First met Red Cliffs in a novel, a TV show, or a game?

cb611.text: We only tell what the records hold. Subscribe to open files with us.
